narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 56.6% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction toward failure. You placed in the second decile, noticeably lower than the average of about 5.8 among accepted students. This weaker academic standing in later years signaled higher risk to the model.

Next, your undergraduate GPA worked in your favor, pulling the prediction toward passing. At 3.30 it sits slightly above the 3.23 average of accepted applicants, giving the model some reassurance about your academic ability.

Finally, your upper-middle family income contributed modestly toward failure. While this bracket is the most common among accepted students (45%), the model still saw it as a slight negative in your overall profile.

Taken together, the lower third-year ranking outweighed your solid GPA and tipped the scales past the acceptance threshold.

What you should do next is straightforward: strengthen the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retake challenging courses to improve your class rank, consider a post-baccalaureate program that demonstrates sustained academic growth, or apply to schools with different admissions models that weigh recent performance differently. These steps can directly address the concerns that led to your rejection. (248 words)
